A. New hyperfine qubit in CaF

In previous work using CaF molecules, coherent interactions and two-qubit gates were demonstrated using a rotational qubit encoding [24,25]. Specifically, two interacting states from two neighboring rotational manifolds, j↑i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 0; mF ¼ 0i and j↓i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1;mF ¼ 0i, were used. Here, we utilize a new noninteracting qubit encoding suitable for storing quantum information. Specifically, our encoding uses the two hyperfine states j1i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1; mF ¼ 0i and j0i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 0; mF ¼ 0i, both from the ground rovibrational manifold X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ [Fig. 3(a)]. These states are predicted to have long coherence times because of the absence of tensor ac Stark shifts and their low magnetic moments. In addition, they are naturally compatible with our error mitigation scheme, as they belong to the dark state manifold T . We note that hyperfine qubit encodings in molecules have been previously proposed for use in quantum information processing [8], and hyperfine coherence times have been measured previously in the bialkali molecules NaK [52], RbCs [53], and NaRb [54]. Very recent work concurrent with ours has also demonstrated a hyperfine qubit encoding in bialkali NaCs molecules trapped in an optical tweezer array [27]. We first demonstrate coherent control over this new hyperfine qubit and show that it has long coherence times. We coherently control the qubit by driving an M1 transition (at approximately 122 MHz) through a two-photon Raman process. Specifically, we use light detuned halfway between the X −A2Π1=2 and X −A2Π3=2 transitions (single-photon detuning of ΔXA ≈2π × 1.1 THz) [Fig. 3(b)]. The two frequencies in the Raman light copropagate and have σþ projections. To demonstrate coherent control, we prepare molecules in j1i and apply Raman light for a variable duration. As shown in Fig. 3(c), we observe Rabi oscillations at ΩR ≈2π × 15 kHz. We next measure the qubit coherence time using a Ramsey sequence consisting of two Raman π=2 pulses separated by a variable duration. To minimize inhomogeneous light shifts between sites due to tweezer trapping light, we operate at a tweezer depth of Uhf ¼ kB × 39ð1Þ μK. By measuring the decay rate of the amplitude of the Ramsey fringe, we find a bare coherence time of T 2 ¼ 19.5ð7Þ ms, which can be increased to T2 ¼ 288ð15Þ ms with a single spin echo. We further extend the coherence time to 1710(60) ms by applying dynamical decoupling with an XY8 pulse sequence (pulse separation of 33.3 ms) [Fig. 3(d)]. In addition to having long coherence times, this hyperfine qubit can be interfaced with the rotational qubit used in

previous work [22,24,25]. Specifically, we have verified that a quantum state can be coherently transferred from the rotational encoding (j↑i; j↓i) to the hyperfine encoding (j1i; j0i) (Appendix I).

C. Erasure conversion and detection of qubit leakage errors induced by blackbody radiation

Having quantified the performance of our composite erasure imaging scheme, we next use it to mitigate a significant error for our hyperfine qubit—leakage into higher vibrational states due to blackbody radiation at room temperature. Specifically, blackbody radiation drives Δv ¼ 1 vibrational-changing E1 transitions, leading to leakage from the qubit states (encoded in v ¼ 0) to the vibrationally excited states E ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 1; N ¼ 1Þ. The estimated leakage rate is Γ01 ≈0.3 s−1 [56], which is a slow but significant source of qubit loss. As we will show, these errors can be converted to population in the bright states F and detected in a site-resolved manner. In other words, the leakage errors can be converted into erasures and detected. To perform erasure conversion, we simply apply v ¼ 1 vibrational repumping light that repumps molecules into the bright manifold F with 98% probability [Fig. 5(a)]. There are, however, two subtleties. First, vibrationally excited molecules in X2Σðv ¼ 1Þ decay back to the ground vibrational manifold X2Σðv ¼ 0Þ at a rate Γ10 ≈5.3 s−1, which is much quicker than the blackbody excitation rate Γ01 ≈0.3 s−1. Therefore, erasure conversion should occur at a rate much faster than Γ10. It is not necessary, however, to detect the error flags in F quickly since they lie in the long-lived ground vibrational manifold. Second, blackbody radiation causes secondary leakage of molecules out of the detectable bright states F into the undetected dark states X2Σðv ¼ 1; N ¼ 0; 2Þ [Fig. 5(b)]. These states then decay both back to F and also to another dark rotational manifold X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 3Þ. We close this leakage pathway by applying rotational repumping light (N ¼ 3 repumper) that brings X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 3Þ molecules back to the error flag manifold F [Fig. 5(b)].

We first experimentally confirm that secondary blackbody leakage is indeed suppressed by N ¼ 3 repumping light. We indeed find that with the extra repumping light, the error flags F have a population lifetime of τ ¼ 13.5ð5Þ s, well exceeding the blackbody-limited lifetime by a factor of approximately 4. The residual loss is attributed to background gas collisions and double blackbody excitation events into dark rotational manifolds with N ≥5 (Appendix J). We next experimentally implement our blackbody erasure conversion scheme and investigate whether it extends qubit population lifetimes and coherence times. We measure the offset and amplitude of Ramsey fringes with and without erasure excision. For these measurements, erasure conversion is repeatedly applied midcircuit, with erasure detection occurring once at the end of the sequence. During the Ramsey hold time, XY8 dynamical decoupling is applied. Regarding qubit population loss, we measure a bare loss rate of γp ¼ 0.30ð1Þ s−1, consistent with the estimated

blackbody excitation rate. Excising erasures, the loss rate decreases to γp;E ¼ 0.14ð1Þ s−1 [Fig. 5(c)]. We find that a loss rate model that incorporates vacuum loss, blackbody excitation, erasure conversion and detection efficiency, and the internal state preparation fidelity agrees well with our measurements [Fig. 5(c)]. We use this model to infer that approximately 80% of blackbody errors are erasure converted and detected correctly (Appendix J). Regarding qubit coherence, we measure a bare loss rate of γc ¼ 0.58ð2Þ s−1, which decreases to γc;E ¼ 0.40ð2Þ s−1

upon excising erasures. This improvement is consistent with the improvement in population loss, suggesting that blackbody radiation does not lead to additional decoherence beyond population loss. Overall, we find that erasure conversion of blackbody errors allows excision of 51(3)% (31(5)%) of all qubit population (coherence) errors, which includes loss due to a finite vacuum lifetime. Looking ahead, because these blackbody erasures can be detected midsequence, they can, in principle, be corrected, as previously demonstrated in molecular ions [55]. For molecular tweezer arrays, blackbody erasures can be removed via reloading a site or by reinitializing the molecular state [57,58].

VII. DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK

In summary, we have demonstrated two error mitigation schemes for state preparation errors and qubit leakage errors. Specifically, we demonstrated (1) a measurementenhanced state preparation scheme that enables robust and record-level fidelities for preparing defect-free and internally pure molecular arrays, and (2) an erasure conversion and detection scheme for blackbody-induced leakage errors of a hyperfine qubit. Both parts of our work represent key new capabilities in the quantum control of molecules. Our measurement-enhanced state preparation work is the first demonstration of removal of internal state errors following midsequence error detection; our erasure conversion work constitutes the first demonstration of erasure conversion in molecules. Our error mitigation work opens several possibilities. First, state preparation fidelities of approximately 95% open the door to quantum simulation of many-body Hamiltonians with low defect rates. In particular, for mesoscopic systems of Oð10Þ particles, we can postselect on perfectly prepared arrays with a tolerable level of data reduction. Second, our work lays the foundations for exploring erasure conversion in the context of quantum error correction with molecular qubits. For quantum error correction, erasure conversion is useful when the dominant errors— often from two-qubit gates—are converted and detected [35]. Our current work concerns erasure conversion of a significant source of leakage errors in noninteracting hyperfine qubits. For quantum memories stored in these qubits, our work could thus substantially

In several experiments including ours [24,25,27], two-qubit gate fidelities were limited by thermal motion within tweezers, which led to variations in the interaction strength and, consequently, gate errors. In addition to the above possibilities opened by our error mitigation results, the new technical capabilities developed in our work also open additional possibilities. First, our new noninteracting hyperfine qubit encoding can be integrated with the previously used interacting rotational encoding, directly enabling applications using three-level systems that include quantum information processing with qutrits, simulation of S ¼ 1 quantum spin models, bosonic t-J models [59], and lattice gauge theory models [60]. Second, our work on detecting blackbody excitations is directly relevant to investigations of molecule-based temperature standards [61]. Third, our work on enhanced tweezer preparation and catching blackbody errors could aid molecular tweezer-based precision measurement experiments [15,16], both through reducing spatial disorder in molecular arrays and through using metrologically useful entangled states such as spin-squeezed states [62,63] that can be naturally generated in interacting defect-free arrays of many molecules [64,65].

APPENDIX A: GENERAL FRAMEWORK FOR SITE-RESOLVED ERROR DETECTION

In this appendix, we describe a general framework for site-resolved errors in optical tweezer arrays of atoms and molecules. This framework provides a unified way to understand the requirements for site-resolved error detection in the following tasks: (1) preparation of defect-free arrays, (2) measurement-enhanced state preparation, and (3) erasure conversion and detection. In atomic and molecular tweezer array experiments, each tweezer site is either empty or occupied by one particle. At each site, the local Hilbert space H consists of j∅i, the state corresponding to an empty site, and the set of all internal states [Fig. 6(a)]. For a particular application, only a target subset of these states T is used. For example, for state preparation, one state in T is used; for encoding a qubit, at least two states from T are needed. Note that while we ignore the motional degree of freedom of a particle within a tweezer, the same framework can be extended to include motional states [30]. For error detection, one encodes the presence of an error as occupation in a set of detectable internal states F (bright

Note that feig could be used to remove errors midsequence or to postselect for error-free instances by excising error-flagged data. When at least one bit of information is encoded in T , errors with a known location are called erasures [33,34]. In particular, population that leaks out of T into other internal states E can be transferred to the error flag states F and subsequently detected. This process is known as erasure conversion [35]. For site-resolved error detection to be practically useful, it must not affect error-free sites. Specifically, for quantum erasure detection, all populations and coherences in T should be minimally affected by detection. We will reserve the term midcircuit for situations when T encodes a qubit and is minimally affected by conversion or detection. In the following, we explicitly show how this framework applies to the following three tasks: (1) preparation of defect-free arrays, (2) measurement-enhanced state preparation, and (3) erasure conversion and detection. For the task of preparing defect-free arrays, the target space T consists of all detectable bright states. In our case, they arethe12 hyperfine states within the rotationalmanifold that permits optical cycling [T ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ]. Because the T are the only laser-coolable states, any site is either in T or in the empty state j∅i. Error detection involves determining empty states, i.e., population in j∅i, without substantially affecting occupied sites (in states T ). This task is accomplished through nondestructive fluorescence detection, which returns a binarized outcome bi, with 1 corresponding to a fluorescing site and 0 corresponding to a dark site. The error flag is given by ei ¼ fðbiÞ ¼ ∼bi since fluorescing sites are filled and hence error-free, while dark sites are empty and thus have occupation errors. Defect-free preparation is accomplished by rearranging error-free or occupied tweezers into the desired configuration. For measurement-enhanced internal state preparation, the target space T consists of a specific dark state. In our specific case described in Sec. V, this state is j−i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; F ¼ 1; mf ¼ −1i, with state preparation errors flagged as population in bright states F ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ. Error detection requires that error-free sites, which have population in j−i, remain unaffected by fluorescence detection of error flags F. Thus, the detection scheme should not cause leakage into other internal states or loss, which in this framework can be thought of as leakage into j∅i. The error detection outcome again consists of bitstrings fbig, with 1 for sites with fluorescence and 0 for dark sites. Here, the mapping to errors is simply ei ¼ fðbiÞ ¼ bi. Internal state preparation errors can then be identified and optionally removed via tweezer rearrangement.

The above two tasks can be viewed as a form of classical generalized erasure detection. For the final case of detecting qubit leakage errors (quantum erasures), the target space T contains at least two states. In our case, these are the dark states j1i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1; mF ¼ 0i and j0i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 0; mF ¼ 0i, as described in Sec. VI A of the main text. Similar to measurement-enhanced state preparation, errors are encoded in the bright states F ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ and detected. The same mapping of error detection bitstrings fbig to error flags feig applies [fðbiÞ ¼ bi]. In our demonstration of erasure conversion of blackbody-induced leakage errors described in Sec. VI C of the main text, blackbody excitation causes leakage into the states E ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 1; N ¼ 1Þ, which are converted into the bright states F ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 1; N ¼ 0Þ with a vibrational repumping laser.

APPENDIX D: INTERNAL STATE PREPARATION PROCEDURE

In this appendix, we provide details on the internal state preparation procedure, which includes optical pumping and microwave transfer.

1. Optical pumping procedure

Our procedure for optical pumping into jD0i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ; J ¼ 3=2; F ¼ 2; mF ¼ −2i involves using light resonant with the X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ → A2Π1=2ðv ¼ 0; J ¼ 1=2; þÞ transition. It involves several steps, with a crucial final step where jD0i is the only hyperfine state in X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ that is dark. In brief, the final optical pumping step uses a single beam containing minimal σþ projection onto the quantization axis set by the magnetic field, which is oriented along the tweezer polarization axis and has a magnitude of B ¼ 3.9 G. The beam contains four frequencies addressing the four hyperfine manifolds in X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ and has a total power of P ¼ 6.4 μW. The tweezer depth is kept at U ¼ kB × 930ð20Þ μK during optical pumping.

2. Microwave transfer procedure

Two population transfers via microwave pulses are used to implement and verify the internal state preparation procedure. Each pulse is performed at a tweezer depth of U ¼ kB × 130ð3Þ μK in a magnetic field of B ¼ 4.4 G oriented at θ ¼ 53° from the tweezer polarization axis. The first pulse transfers population from jD0i to j−i ¼ jX2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 0Þ; J ¼ 1=2; F ¼ 1; mF ¼ −1i and the second from j−i to j↑i. Each utilizes a composite 90y180x90y pulse sequence that increases the robustness to microwave power fluctuations. We also shape the amplitude of each pulse using a Gaussian envelope that is truncated at 3 ﬃﬃ 2 p σ, where σ is the Gaussian width.

The peak Rabi frequency during the first (second) composite pulse is Ω ≈2π × 900 kHz (Ω ≈2π × 300 kHz), with a total pulse duration of 3.7 μs (11.0 μs).

APPENDIX E: RAPID IMAGING, COMPOSITE ERASURE DETECTION, AND THEIR CHARACTERIZATION

1. Rapid imaging procedure

All rapid imaging configurations use light containing four frequency components resonant with the four resolved hyperfine transitions between the X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ and A2Π1=2ðv¼0;J¼1=2;þÞ manifolds. Vibrational repumpers for X2Σðv ¼ 1; 2; 3; N ¼ 1Þ and a rotational repumper for X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 3Þ are simultaneously applied. The resonant X-A light is delivered by two retroreflected beams with a total intensity of I ¼ 4.5 mW=cm2 and a hyperfine power ratio of 5∶2.7∶1.1∶3.8. The v ¼ 1 and N ¼ 3 repumpers are delivered along the same path as the X-A light and are retroreflected; the v ¼ 2, 3 repumping light is delivered with a single beam. The internal state error detection sequence (rapid resonant imaging) is composed of a 1-ms tweezer depth ramp from U ¼ kB × 130ð3Þ μK to U ¼ kB × 930ð20Þ μK, a rapid resonant image (3 ms), and a 1-ms tweezer ramp back to U ¼ kB × 130ð3Þ μK. This image occurs at (B ¼ 4.4 G, θ ¼ 53°). The blackbody error detection and composite erasure image sequences are composed of a 1-ms tweezer depth ramp from U ¼ kB × 39ð1Þ μK to U ¼ kB × 930ð20Þ μK, a rapid resonant image (3 ms), and a 1-ms tweezer ramp back to U ¼ kB × 39ð1Þ μK. Halfway through the erasure image, a 40-μs X-B Raman π pulse realizes a spin echo in the hyperfine qubit manifold. Composite erasure imaging occurs at (B ¼ 2.0 G, θ ¼ 90°), which is also a pseudomagic configuration for the rotational qubit.

2. Photon scattering rate

For rapid resonant imaging, the X-A photon scattering rate is determined from the number of photons collected by the camera. Image histograms are constructed by postselecting for molecules that survive the rapid resonant image; this ensures that the imaging lifetime, which is comparable to the image duration, does not affect the scattering rate measurement. We find that approximately 24 photons are collected by the camera during the 3-ms rapid resonant image. Incorporating the microscope objective collection efficiency and optical losses along the imaging path gives a scattering rate of Rscat ≈1.6 × 105 s−1. We have compared this scattering rate with that obtained using a Bloch equation simulation using the measured hyperfine balance and detunings [67,71]. APPENDIX G: GENERATING DEFECT-FREE AND INTERNALLY PURE ARRAYS VIA REARRANGEMENT

In this appendix, we describe our protocol for preparing defect-free and internally pure arrays of molecules and the procedure to determine the array preparation fidelities. Array preparation involves five steps. (1) A nondestructive image of a stochastically filled array of molecules is taken. Empty tweezers are turned off, and occupied tweezers are rearranged into a uniformly spaced defectfree (occupation) array, as described in our earlier work [24]. (2) A second nondestructive image is taken to verify successful rearrangement. This image is used to identify occupied tweezers. (3) Our measurementenhanced internal state preparation procedure is applied, producing an error image. This image is used to identify tweezer instances with state preparation errors. (4) Another round of rearrangement is applied, replacing tweezer instances flagged as having an error with error-free and occupied tweezers. For each shot, the target array length equals the number of tweezers identified to be occupied and error-free. (5) Population is transferred from the target internal state T to F for destructive readout. Next, we extract the raw success probability Pn;raw of generating a defect-free and internally pure array of at least n molecules starting from the leftmost tweezer. This probability is conditioned on identifying at least n occupied and error-free tweezers. Since defect-free arrays can be shortened deterministically and with 100% probability by simply dropping tweezers, Pn;raw gives the fidelity of preparing a defect-free, internally pure array of n molecules. We next correct for measurement errors. The threshold used for the final destructive image keeps the false-positive probability negligible (ϵ01 < 0.1%) and the false-negative probability small (ϵ10 ¼ 1.2%). In this limit, the measurement-corrected success rate is

Pn ¼ Pn;raw ð1 −ϵ10Þn : ðG1Þ

APPENDIX H: MEASURING AND MODELING LIFETIME OF X2Σðv = 0;N = 1;3Þ MOLECULES

Since molecules in F ¼ X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1Þ serve as error flags, it is important to quantify their population lifetime, which we measure in the pseudomagic configuration [U ¼ kB × 39ð1Þ μK, B ¼ 2.0 G]. As discussed in the main text, molecules in the detection manifold F that leak to X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 3Þ because of blackbody excitation can be repumped back into F using a rotational repumper, which is applied during the final destructive image. We model population loss in F using a rate equation model that includes X2Σðv ¼ 0Þ rotational states with odd N for N ≤13, X2Σðv ¼ 1Þ rotational states with even N for N ≤13, and vacuum loss. We further assume that the population is initially distributed uniformly across all hyperfine states in F and all blackbody excitations and that decays keep populations uniformly distributed within each N manifold. Figure 10 shows the measured X2Σðv ¼ 0; N ¼ 1; 3Þ total population decay and inferred populations in various rovibrational manifolds. Fitting our rate equation model to the data yields a vacuum loss rate of γvac ¼ 0.047ð3Þ s−1.

Our model, along with the fitted vacuum loss rate, allows us to infer populations in various rovibrational manifolds (Fig. 10) and attribute losses. At the measured lifetime of τ ¼ 13.5ð5Þ s, our model predicts of the molecules that survive vacuum loss, 32% of population is missed in the final readout image, of which 5% is due to equilibration with states in v ¼ 1 and 27% is due to a multistep excitation and decay process that populates v ¼ 0, N > 5 states.

APPENDIX I: QUBIT TRANSFER BETWEEN ROTATIONAL AND HYPERFINE ENCODINGS

In this appendix, we provide supplemental information and data showing compatibility between our hyperfine qubit encoding used for erasure conversion and the previously used rotational encoding where a two-qubit gate has been demonstrated. The building blocks for transferring a qubit between the rotational encoding and the hyperfine encoding are π pulses along the Raman and microwave transitions [Fig. 12(a)]. For these data, due to technical limitations, Raman light detuned from the X −B transition was used. Specifically, the Raman light is detuned halfway between the X2ΣðN ¼ 0Þ →B2ΣðN ¼ 1; J ¼ 1=2Þ and X2ΣðN ¼ 0Þ→B2ΣðN ¼1;J¼3=2Þ transitions. This process results in a single-photon detuning of 500 MHz for optical transitions resonant with the hyperfine qubit states. For this scheme, Qπ is measured to be 37(3). We characterize the ability to transfer arbitrary states between the rotational (j↑i −j↓i) and hyperfine encoding (j↓i −j0i) by comparing single-particle coherence after four different Ramsey sequences: two in which no transfer occurs and two in which a single transfer occurs [Fig. 12(b)]. We find that the decrease in single-particle coherence is consistent with zero after one round of transfer [Figs. 12(c) and 12(d)]. To more precisely estimate the transfer efficiency, we measure single-particle coherence as a function of repeated transfers between the two different qubit encodings [Fig. 12(e)]. From these measurements, we

find a transfer fidelity of f ¼ 0.951ð2Þ, limited by offresonant scattering of the Raman light. We find that offresonant scattering accounts for 89(9)% of the infidelity, with the remaining amount consistent with the separately measured microwave transfer infidelity. We therefore expect the transfer fidelity to improve to f ≈0.995 when using optimally detuned Raman light on the X-A transition.

# Raman Sideband Cooling of Molecules in an Optical Tweezer Array

Yukai Lu,1, 2, ∗Samuel J. Li,1, ∗Connor M. Holland,1, ∗and Lawrence W. Cheuk1, †

1Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA (Dated: June 6, 2023)

Ultracold molecules, because of their rich internal structures and interactions, have been proposed as a promising platform for quantum science and precision measurement. Direct laser-cooling promises to be a rapid and efficient way to bring molecules to ultracold temperatures. For trapped molecules, laser-cooling to the quantum motional ground state remains an outstanding challenge. A technique capable of reaching the motional ground state is Raman sideband cooling, first demonstrated in trapped ions and atoms. In this work, we demonstrate for the first time Raman sideband cooling of molecules. Specifically, we demonstrate 3D Raman cooling for single CaF molecules trapped in an optical tweezer array, achieving average radial (axial) motional occupation as low as ¯nr = 0.27(7) (¯nz = 7.0(10)). Notably, we measure a 1D ground state fraction as high as 0.79(4), and a motional entropy per particle of s = 4.9(3), the lowest reported for laser-cooled molecules to date. These lower temperatures could enable longer coherence times and higher fidelity molecular qubit gates desirable for quantum information processing and quantum simulation. With further improvements, Raman cooling could also be a new route towards molecular quantum degeneracy applicable to many laser-coolable molecular species including polyatomic ones.

Ultracold molecules have been proposed as a new platform for exploring many areas in physics ranging from simulation of quantum many-body Hamiltonians, to quantum information processing, to precision measurements in searches for physics beyond the Standard Model [1–4]. Yet, cooling and fully controlling molecules have been long-standing experimental challenges. One route to produce ultracold molecules is via assembly from atoms, for which cooling techniques are well-developed. This approach has successfully been used to produce bialkali molecules, enabling explorations in ultracold chemistry [5, 6] and the creation of quantum-degenerate molecular gases well-suited for studying long-ranged interacting many-body systems [7, 8]. In contrast to assembly from ultracold atoms, methods that directly cool could be broadly applicable to a large variety of molecular species including polyatomic ones. In particular, direct laser-cooling of molecules has seen great advances recently. Starting with molecular magneto-optical traps near the Doppler limit of ∼100 µK [9–13], sub-Doppler cooling techniques have allowed experiments to enter into the µK regime [10, 13– 19]. Importantly, sub-Doppler cooling has enabled optically trapped molecular samples with record densities [14, 18, 20] and arrays of single molecules trapped in optical tweezers [21–23]. Access to molecular samples at even lower temperatures could enable new possibilities. For example, molecular tweezer arrays have recently emerged as a promising platform for quantum science. Notably, recent work has shown high-fidelity control over molecular positions and internal states, coherent dipolar interactions, and implementation of an entangling two-qubit gate [22, 23]. Yet, residual thermal motion limits the achievable coherence times and gate fidelities. These limitations can be largely

eliminated by cooling to the motional ground state. One technique capable of cooling to the motional ground state is Raman sideband cooling (RSC) [24]. First, a Raman process transfers a molecule initially in internal state |↑⟩to |↓⟩while removing ∆n quanta of motional energy. Subsequently, optical pumping reinitializes the internal state to |↑⟩while largely preserving the motional state. By iterating over these two steps, cooling is achieved. RSC was first proposed and demonstrated for trapped ions and atoms in optical lattices [25–27], and has since been used to cool single atoms in tweezer traps to their motional ground states [28, 29], for imaging in quantum gas microscopes [30, 31], and to produce single molecules via assembly from two RSC-cooled atoms [32– 34]. RSC also provides a rapid and efficient (low-loss) all-optical method to create atomic Bose-Einstein condensates [35, 36], circumventing the need for evaporation. Raman sideband cooling of optically trapped and lasercooled molecules faces two main challenges that arise from the complex internal structure of molecules [37]. First, state-dependent optical trapping leads to inhomogeneous broadening of Raman transitions, preventing resolved addressing of cooling sidebands and decreasing transfer efficiency. Second, efficient optical pumping is difficult because of the large number of molecular states and the degradation of free-space selection rules in deep optical traps. In this work, we demonstrate Raman sideband cooling of molecules for the first time. We overcome the above challenges by devising a RSC scheme for CaF molecules that provides both narrow Raman transitions and efficient optical pumping. Our scheme does not require high magnetic fields, in contrast to the one proposed in [37]. We demonstrate 3D Raman cooling for CaF molecules trapped in an optical tweezer array and achieve average

Along the radial direction, the ∆nr = ±1 sidebands are well-resolved. In our RAC scheme, since ∆nr = −2 sidebands are addressed, molecules can accumulate in nr = 1, limiting the radial ground state fraction. To circumvent this while maintaining net cooling, we apply an additional radial cooling sequence, where we interlace radial cooling cycles that separately address the ∆nr = −2 and ∆nr = −1 sidebands (Fig. 4(c)). With an additional 30 cycles of interlaced radial cooling (IRC), we observe that the 1D radial ground state fraction increases to P0 = 0.79(4), corresponding to an average radial occupation of ¯nr = 0.27(7) ( ˜Tr = 0.65(9)). Because the axial direction is not cooled during IRC, the axial temperature increases to ˜Tz = 13.5(14) (¯nz = 13.0(14)), still below the initial temperature. When the motion is highly quantized, as in our case, a useful figure-of-merit in addition to temperature is the motional entropy. This quantifies how many motional states are populated and indicates the level of control over the initial motional state. With RAC, we obtain a motional entropy per particle of s = 5.2+0.5 −0.4 compared

to s = 7.5+0.8 −0.7 before cooling. With IRC, we further reduce the motional entropy per particle to s = 4.9(3), the lowest reported to date for laser-cooled molecules. Since most of the entropy is in the axial motion, lower entropies and temperatures could be reached with increased axial confinement and further optimized Raman pulse sequences [42–44]. The motional entropy also allows us to quantify the efficiency of our Raman cooling scheme. In evaporative cooling of atomic and molecular gases, a common efficiency metric is γ = −d ln(PSD)/d ln(N) where N is the particle number, and PSD is the phase space density [45– 48]. One can generalize this metric to γq = ds/d ln(N), where s is the motional entropy per particle [39]. γq coincides with γ in the classical regime and is convenient when in the highly quantized regime. Using our loss measurements, we estimate that γq = 70(28) for RAC, indicating highly efficient cooling with little loss. Our demonstration of Raman sideband cooling of molecules in this work opens up several new possibilities. In the near term, the lower temperatures achieved could significantly improve coherence times and provide more coherent dipolar interactions between molecules, enabling high-fidelity quantum gates and quantum simulation with long evolution times. Longer term, our work opens the door to direct laser-cooling of trapped molecules to their 3D motional ground states. This would be a key step towards full quantum control of molecules, and could enable efficient production of ensembles with low motional entropy suited for quantum simulation of itinerant many-body systems. Potentially, this could provide an all-optical route towards quantum degeneracy [35, 36] that may be broadly applicable to other lasercoolable molecules including polyatomic ones.

## METHODS

Preparation of Molecules

CaF molecules in the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold are created in a single-stage cryogenic buffer gas cell [49], slowed via chirped slowing, and loaded into a DC magneto-optical trap (MOT). The MOT is subsequently switched off, Λ-cooling is applied, and the molecules are loaded into an optical dipole trap (ODT) with the aid of a repulsive ring trap in the presence of Λ- cooling [50]. The molecules are optically transported and loaded into a reconfigurable array of 37 optical tweezers, which are created with focused laser beams of 781 nm light projected vertically through a microscope objective [38]. For normalization, after tweezer loading, the occupation of the tweezers are detected non-destructively with Λ-imaging [22]. After non-destructive detection, the molecules are spread out over all 12 hyperfine states in the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold.

State-Resolved Detection

To probe the population in |↓⟩, we first lower the trap depth to UMW = kB × 130(3) µK and rotate the magnetic field (B = 4.4 G) to θ = 53◦. Microwaves at ∼ 20.5 GHz are used to transfer the population from |↓⟩= |N = 1, J = 3/2, F = 1, mF = 0⟩ to |N = 0, J = 1/2, F = 1, mF = −1⟩ via a Landau- Zener sweep. A pulse of light resonant with the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) → A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) transition removes any molecules remaining in X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) [22, 38]. A second Landau-Zener microwave sweep transfers molecules into |N = 1, J = 1/2, F = 0, mF = 0⟩. Finally, the population is measured via Λ-imaging [14], which detects all molecules in X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1). An analogous approach is used to measure population in |↑⟩.

Optical Pumping

For optical pumping at θ = 0◦, we use a single beam (OP) in the radial (horizontal) plane. The beam makes an angle of 42◦relative to the tweezer polarization axis ˆε (ˆx). It is optimized to have minimal σ+ component along the quantization axis set by the magnetic field (along ˆx at θ = 0◦). For the data exploring optical pumping at the magic angle θ = θm (Fig. 2(b,c)), we use a second optical pumping beam (OP2) propagating along ˆy. This beam is optimized to have minimal σ+ component along the quantization axis set by the magnetic field.

Raman Coupling

To achieve Raman coupling between |↑⟩and |↓⟩, we use light with two frequency components ω1 and ω2 detuned near the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) −B2Σ(v = 0, N = 0) transition (single-photon detuning of ∆= −2π × 42 GHz). ω1(ω2) nominally couples to |↑⟩(|↓⟩). These components are generated by acousto-optical modulators (AOMs), allowing the two-photon detuning δ to be varied. To achieve motional coupling in the radial (horizontal) xy-plane, we send beams R1 and R2 along the ˆx + ˆy and ˆx −ˆy directions, respectively. R1(R2) carries a single frequency component ω1(ω2) and is linearly polarized vertically along ˆz. The two beams are optionally retroreflected. The retro-reflections are controlled by shutters that can be controlled mid-sequence. To address axial motion, we send beams R3 and R4 along −ˆz and ˆz, respectively. The beam R3 is linearly polarized along ˆy, while R4 is linearly polarized perpendicular to θ = θm.

Spectroscopy Sequences

We use the following sequence for the data presented in Fig. 2(a). First, molecules are pumped into |↑⟩by turning on OP for 2 ms in a bias magnetic field of B = 4.4 G at θ = 0◦. Next, the tweezer depth is decreased to UR and the magnetic field is rotated to the desired angle θ. Both ω1 and ω2 are delivered via a single vertical beam R4 along the tweezer axis. A Raman pulse is applied for 170 µs with an estimated two-photon Rabi coupling of ΩR ≈2π × 3 kHz. Finally, the population in |↓⟩is measured. For all spectra in Figs. 3 and 4, the radial Raman beams R1 and R2 are not retro-reflected. All spectra in Fig. 3 are taken in a bias field of B = 4.4 G at θ = 0◦. For the radial spectrum in Fig. 3(a), radial beams R1 and R2 are applied for 1 ms, probing the radial direction ˆy. For the axial spectrum in Fig. 3(b), ω1 is delivered via R3 and ω2 via R4, and the beams are applied for 1 ms. All spectra in Fig. 4 are taken in a magnetic field of B = 5.5 G at θ = θm. For radial spectra in Fig. 4(a,c), R1 and R2 are used. The beams are applied for 30 µs (carrier) or 50 µs (∆nr = ±1 sidebands), with ΩR ≈2π× 20 kHz. For axial spectra in Fig. 4(b,d), ω1 is delivered via R3 and ω2 via R4. The beams are applied for 100 µs, with an estimated Rabi frequency of ΩR ≈2π × 20 kHz.

Cooling Sequences

Prior to Raman sideband cooling, we optically pump molecules into |↑⟩by applying beam OP for 2 ms. For the radial/axial cooling sequence (RAC), both radial beams R1 and R2 are on and retro-reflected. Axially, we send ω1 into R3, and ω2 into R4. We perform Raman

transfer on the radial ∆nr = −2 sideband for 150 µs, and optical pumping with OP for 150 µs. The Raman transfer occurs at tweezer depth UR, and the optical pumping occurs at depth U0. The tweezer depth ramps occur over 200 µs between each of these steps.

For the interlaced radial cooling sequence (IRC), we only turn on radial beams R1 and R2, with R2 retroreflected. Raman transfer on the ∆nr = −2 (∆nr = −1) sideband occurs for 150 µs (300 µs).

## I. BRIGHT STATE ADMIXTURE DUE TO TRAPPING LIGHT

In this section, we discuss the bright state admixture into the stretched states |±⟩= |F = 2, mF = ±2⟩in the X(v = 0, N = 1) manifold, relevant to the discussion of optical pumping in the main text. The states {|+⟩, |−⟩} can be prepared via optical pumping as each is dark to {σ+, σ−} and π light addressing the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) −A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) transition. For example, one can optically pump into |+⟩by applying light devoid of a σ−component. In the presence of tweezer light, the free space eigenstates |±⟩= |F = 2, mF = ±2⟩are perturbed and become slightly modified eigenstates e± containing other free-space eigenstates that are bright to σ± or π light. For example, the in-trap eigenstate e+ can be decomposed into free-space eigenstates as e+ = |+⟩+ ϵi |+i⟩, where |+i⟩are other N = 1 states that are bright to σ+ or π light. The bright state population admixture M = P

i |ϵi|2 therefore quantifies the brightness of e+

to optical pumping light, which determines the quality of optical pumping. To determine whether e+ or e− is better for optical pumping, we numerically compute M in the presence of optical tweezer light at 781 nm. Specifically, we compute M via M± = 1 − ⟨±|e±⟩ 2 both as a function of the tweezer depth (U) and as a function of the angle (θ) between the bias magnetic field and the tweezer polarization axis. As shown in Fig. S1, the darkness is maximal at 00◦, and e− is darker than e+ across all relevant depths. To elaborate, while e± are equivalent choices at zero magnetic field, in the presence of a magnetic field and optical trapping light, the two behave differently. ## II. HEATING DURING OPTICAL PUMPING

In free-space, each photon emitted or absorbed will increase the motional energy by an amount ER = ℏ2k2/2m = h × 9.2 kHz. In our optical pumping configuration, an average of 19 total photons are required to pump the molecule from |↓⟩to |↑⟩. In terms of radial motional quanta, this leads to a heating of ∆nr ∼ 19ER/(ℏωr) = 0.93. In addition to this recoil heating, projection heating occurs as the molecule transitions between the various N = 1 hyperfine states in the presence of differing trapping potentials [1]. Projection heating worsens with increasing motional quantum number (Fig. S2). Starting from our initial ˜Tr = 1.8

## III. RAMAN SIDEBAND BROADENING MECHANISMS AND ESTIMATES

In this section, we describe and estimate various mechanisms that broaden Raman spectra. In an ideal scenario, the internal states |↑⟩and |↓⟩ experience identical harmonic potentials with trapping frequency ω, giving rise to motional states separated in energy by ℏω. Motional changing transitions of the form |↑, ni⟩→|↑, nf = ni + ∆n⟩can be driven by addressing Raman sidebands using a two-photon detuning δ of

ℏδ(∆n) = E0 + ℏω∆n, (1)

where E0 is the carrier (∆n = 0) energy separation. In this idealized approximation, motional changing transitions are grouped into sidebands which are spaced by multiples of ℏω about the carrier.

## A. Trap Anharmonicity and Differential Trapping

Trapping anharmonicity, which arises from the Gaussian trapping profile of the tweezer beams, and statedependent ac Stark shifts, which arises from the complex internal structure of molecules, lead to departures from this ideal scenario. In particular, trapping anharmonicity leads to motional state-dependent sideband spacing, while differential ac Stark shifts lead to motional statedependent carrier energies and the sideband spacings. ## C. Accounting of Raman Broadening

In Table S1, we summarize the various broadening contributions to the (∆n = 0) carrier linewidth both in the cooling (θ = 0◦) and magic (θ = θm) configurations. ## C. Unresolved Thermometry in the Doppler Limit along the Axial Direction

Since the axial trapping frequencies are smaller than the radial ones, the axial sidebands are more closely spaced and are challenging to resolve. Furthermore, because the axial Lamb-Dicke parameter is large, there is significant and non-uniform coupling to many sidebands, complicating sideband thermometry. Specifically, extracting the ground state fraction and determining axial temperatures using sideband asymmetry are challenging. To perform robust axial thermometry, we instead measure Raman spectra far from the carrier and in the unresolved regime. Specifically, we increase the Raman Rabi coupling until high-order sidebands become unresolved and blend into the Gaussian-shaped wings. The resulting wings are fit to a Gaussian, and an axial temperature is extracted by comparing the fit to a numerical simulation. This method is agnostic to many details of the axial trapping potential and is equivalent to two-photon Doppler spectroscopy.

## VI. DISCUSSION OF ENTROPY AND TEMPERATURE

In general, entropy encodes the amount of randomness in a system. From an information theory perspective, entropy quantifies the imperfect knowledge of the precise quantum state of a system, and therefore also describes the degree of control one has over a quantum system. Therefore, motional entropy per particle, rather than absolute temperatures and phase space densities, is a more universal metric for quantifying cooling and quantum control. In this section, we will discuss i) motional entropy for a trapped particle, ii) the relation of motional entropy to phase space density, and iii) distribution of total entropy for the specific case of a molecular tweezer array.

## B. Relation of Entropy to Phase Space Density

For a classical gas at temperature T, the entropy per particle s is given by the Sackur-Tetrode equation as

s = −ln (PSD) + 5

These approach the classical expression at high temperature/entropies. For reference, in a homogeneous non-interacting 3D Bose gas, Bose-Einstein condensation occurs at PSD = 2.612 with a corresponding entropy per particle of s = 1.283. For a single component non-interacing Fermi gas in 3D, PSD = 4/(3√π(T/TF )3/2), where TF is the Fermi temperature. At T/TF = 1, PSD = 0.752 and s = 2.95. For our experiment, after Raman cooling, the motional entropy remains above these values at s ≈5, well within the classical regime. In terms of the cooling efficiency, the commonly used evaporative efficiency γ = −d ln(PSD)/d ln(N) in the classical regime can be written in terms of entropy per particle as γ = ds/d ln(N). This coincides with the definition γq = ds/d ln(N) defined in the main text.

## C. Distribution of Total Entropy in a Molecular Tweezer Array

Here, we discuss the distribution of total entropy in the specific case of a molecular tweezer array. In addition to motional states, a molecular tweezer array contains additional degrees of freedom, in which entropy can be stored. Specifically, entropy can be stored in the spatial configuration of the molecules and the internal state distribution of the molecules. For the purposes of quantifying quantum control over a many-body quantum system, one must therefore compute the total entropy per particle stot stored over all these degrees of freedom. This allows a fair comparison to bulk molecular samples. In the following, we outline how to estimate stot and provide a value that is achievable with our latest Raman cooling results and previous work on initializing arbitrary 1D molecular tweezer arrays. We assume that the different tweezer sites are uncorrelated initially. For each tweezer site, the Hilbert space contains the state ∅corresponding to an empty tweezer without a molecule, and the states {|i, n⟩}, corresponding to a molecule in internal state i and motional state N within an occupied tweezer. In the next sections, we provide expressions for computing the various entropy contributions.

# A Blue-Detuned Magneto-Optical Trap of CaF Molecules

Samuel J. Li,1, ∗Connor M. Holland,1, ∗Yukai Lu,1, 2 and Lawrence W. Cheuk1, †

1Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA (Dated: November 10, 2023)

A key method to produce trapped and laser-cooled molecules is the magneto-optical trap (MOT), which is conventionally created using light red-detuned from an optical transition. In this work, we report a MOT for CaF molecules created using blue-detuned light. The blue-detuned MOT (BDM) achieves temperatures well below the Doppler limit, and provides the highest densities and phase-space densities reported to date in CaF MOTs. We observe short BDM lifetimes at high magnetic field gradients, preventing magnetic compression as a means to increase densities. By directly measuring the BDM restoring force, we find that the short lifetimes are explained by low effective trap depths. Notably, we find sub-mK depths at typical magnetic gradients, in contrast to ∼50 mK depths in red molecular MOTs and ∼0.5 K depths in red atomic MOTs.

Laser-cooled molecules are a promising platform for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, studies of ultracold molecular collisions, and precision probes of physics beyond the Standard Model [1–4]. These applications all benefit from trapped molecular samples that are cold and dense. A workhorse technology for producing trapped laser-cooled atoms and molecules is the magneto-optical trap (MOT), where a magnetic gradient in combination with near-resonant light provides both cooling and spatial confinement. Starting with the first molecular MOTs of SrF [5, 6], MOTs have been demonstrated in other diatomic and polyatomic molecules [7–10]. These developments have enabled trapping of molecules in conservative optical and magnetic traps [11–15], the production of arrays of single molecules [16, 17], explorations of molecular collisions in the ultracold regime [18–20], and observations of coherent electric dipolar interactions and entanglement of molecules [21, 22].

Conventionally, molecular MOTs are created using light red-detuned from an optical transition. They primarily rely on Doppler cooling and achieve temperatures near the Doppler limit TD = ℏΓ/(2kB), where Γ is the excited state linewidth. To achieve the optical cycling needed for laser-cooling, the cooling light addresses a rotational-lowering transition [23] (e.g. N = 1 →N ′ = 0 transition, where N denotes the rotational quantum number). In these so-called type-II systems, the number of excited states is less than or equal to the number of ground states. As pointed out in [24], with reddetuned light, type-II systems experience Doppler cooling at high velocities but sub-Doppler heating at low velocities. With blue-detuned light, Doppler heating and sub-Doppler cooling occur instead [7, 13, 24–26]. It was subsequently realized that blue-detuned MOTs (BDMs), which offer spatial confinement in addition to sub-Doppler cooling, are possible [27–29]. The first BDM was realized with Rb atoms [27]; recently, molecular BDMs of YO [30] and SrF [20] have been created.

In this work, we demonstrate a BDM of CaF molecules, producing the coldest and densest CaF MOT reported to date. Our work starts with a conventional red-detuned MOT of CaF loaded from a cryogenic buffer gas beam. The red MOT utilizes a DC quadrupolar magnetic field (symmetry axis along ˆz) and laser-cooling light reddetuned from the X 2Σ(N = 1) →A 2Π1/2(J = 1/2, +) transition. The light is sent along three orthogonal directions and consists of four frequency components nominally addressing the four ground hyperfine manifolds. The polarizations and frequency detunings of the components are shown in Fig. 1(a,i). Initially, the red-detuned MOT captures molecules at an axial magnetic gradient B′ z = 26 G/cm. Subsequently, the MOT is compressed by ramping the gradient to B′ z = 104 G/cm [11, 32] while simultaneously ramping down the light intensity. This produces a sample with a Gaussian size of σ = 680(30) µm and a temperature of T = 3.9(4) mK. Since BDMs can have low capture velocities [24, 27– 29], we perform further cooling [20, 30]. We switch off the magnetic gradient and immediately perform Λ-enhanced gray molasses cooling [20, 25, 30] to reach a temperature

Subsequently, molecules are captured into the BDM, which uses light blue-detuned to the X 2Σ(N = 1) → A 2Π1/2(J = 1/2, +) transition. Empirically, we have found two BDM schemes: one with four frequencies addressing all four ground hyperfine manifolds, and another with two frequencies (Fig. 1(a,ii,iii)). The first scheme is used for initial loading; the second scheme, which we call Λ-BDM, is used to produce the densest and coldest samples. Initially, we transfer molecules into the four-frequency BDM with a magnetic gradient of B′ z = 14.6 G/cm and an overall frequency detuning of ≈20 MHz (details in [31]). At optimal parameters, the transfer efficiency from the Λ-cooled cloud is ≈70%. Notably, the BDM rapidly reaches its equilibrium size over a 1/e time of 7.9(4) ms. At equilibrium, the axial (radial) size is σz = 294(2) µm (σr = 215(2) µm), and the axial (radial) temperature is Tz = 195(5) µK (Tr = 186(12) µK). The corresponding mean size is σ = σ2/3 r σ1/3 z = 239(2) µm and the mean temperature is T = T 2/3 r T 1/3 z = 189(8) µK, around the Doppler limit of TD = 200 µK. The equilibration time is similar to that reported for SrF and is significantly faster than observed in YO (∼50 ms). We attribute the rapid equilibration to the high photon scattering rate, which we measure to be Γsc = 2.0(2) × 106 s−1 [31]. Although this high scattering rate could provide large trapping and damping forces, it limits the achievable temperature. To reach lower temperatures, we subsequently switch to the two-frequency Λ-BDM configuration (Fig. 1(a,iii)) with light addressing the highest (J = 3/2, F = 2) and lowest (J = 1/2, F = 1−) hyperfine manifolds. The optimal gradient is therefore a compromise between minimizing σ and T and maximizing τ. Empirically, the smallest sizes occur at B′ z = 27 G/cm (σ = 172(4) µm, T = 60(4) µK), the lowest temperatures at B′ z = 6.2 G/cm (σ = 277(5) µm, T = 31(1) µK), and the highest peak phase space density (PSD) at B′ z = 14.6 G/cm (σ = 188(3) µm, T = 39(2) µK). To investigate the origin of the short lifetimes at high gradients, we first examine the dependence of the restoring force on B′ z, since an insufficient restoring force could lead to loss. Assuming Hooke’s law and constant velocity damping, the spring constant k can be obtained from T and σ via keff = kBT/σ2 [31]. In Fig. 3(d), we show ˜keff = keff/kB versus B′ z for both the radial and axial directions. At gradients below B′ z ≈10 G/cm, ˜keff is linear in B′ z, as expected, and has values similar to those reported for YO [30]. At higher gradients, ˜keff appears to saturate, indicating that the average restoring force decreases. Because molecules experience an average magnetic field that grows with gradient as p

B′z, the saturation of ˜keff suggests that F(B) is significantly sub-linear in B at higher magnetic fields.

To test this hypothesis, we next directly measure F(B). We create dense and cold samples by loading a Λ-BDM and subsequently applying free-space Λ-cooling. We then impart an initial velocity of v0 ≈200 mm/s in the radial direction by pulsing on a beam resonant with the X2Σ(N = 1) →B2Σ(N = 0) transition. We next apply a uniform magnetic field ⃗B along the push direction ( ⃗B ∥⃗v0) and switch on the Λ-BDM light for a variable duration t. For each t, we measure the velocity v via time-of-flight expansion. By fitting to an exponential decay with an offset, v(t) = Ae−αt + v∞, we extract the damping coefficient α and the terminal velocity v∞. The restoring force F(B) is then obtained via F = m α v∞. To determine v∞more accurately, we perform a second set of measurements where the push beam is not applied and the molecules start with v0 = 0 (see [31] for details).

In Fig. 4(a,b), we show the extracted damping curve α(B) and acceleration curve a(B) = F(B)/m. For a(B), we observe the expected sign change when reversing the magnetic field. We also find that α(B) and a(B) are significant only when |B| < 1 G. Furthermore, the restoring force is linear only for |B| < 0.5 G. At a gradient of B′ z = 20 G/cm, this magnetic field range corresponds to a radial size of 0.5 mm. The acceleration curve a(B) provides an explanation of the short lifetimes observed at high gradients. In short, we find that the effective BDM trap depth becomes comparable to the molecular temperatures at high gradients, leading to loss. In detail, using a(B), we define an effective conservative trapping potential U(x) = −m R a(B(x))dx along the radial and axial directions [34]. It follows that both the spatial scale and the magnitude of U(x) scale inversely with B′ z (Fig. 4(c)). In other words, both the size and depth of the effective trap decrease with B′ z. To extract an effective depth, we assume that U(x) is of a Gaussian form given by U(x) = −U0 exp [−x2/(2d2)], where U0 is the maximum trap depth and d the Gaussian spatial width. Fitting a(B), we obtain a trap depth of U0(B′ z) = kB×4.6(10) mK·(G/cm)/B′ z, and a trap size of d(B′ z) = 0.62(4) G/B′ z. Notably, at a typical gradient of

20 G/cm, U0 = kB ×230(50) µK, which is only four times higher than the observed temperature. These trap depths are much smaller than the ∼50 mK depths reported for red-detuned molecular MOTs [6, 28, 33] and ∼0.5 K depths reported for red-detuned atomic MOTs [35]. To further support our hypothesis that the short lifetimes arise from insufficient trap depths, we quantitatively examine both the damping α and the local temperature-to-trap-depth ratio η(x) = (kBT)/U(x). Using the measured dependences of σ and T on B′ z (Fig. 3), we perform Monte-Carlo simulations to obtain ensemble-averaged values of ⟨η⟩and ⟨α⟩(Fig. 4(d,e)) [31]. We observe that ⟨α⟩, which determines the average cooling rate, varies by no more than 20% over experimentally relevant gradients. On the other hand, ⟨η⟩varies significantly and even exceeds unity. Because the fraction of particles above the local trap depth is given by exp(−1/η), the dependence of ⟨η⟩on B′ z suggests that a shallow trap depth (insufficient restoring force), rather than the lack of velocity damping, is the primary cause of loss at high gradients. Semi-quantitatively, the loss rate due to finite trap depth can be estimated as C P i⟨αi exp(−1/ηi)⟩, where i sums over the radial and axial directions and C is a constant of order O(0.1) [31]. As shown in the inset of Fig. 4(e), this loss model (with two additional parameters to describe background loss and minimum escape time) qualitatively reproduces the observed lifetime dependence on B′ z. In summary, we have demonstrated a blue-detuned MOT of CaF molecules that reaches temperatures significantly below the Doppler limit. Specifically, the Λ- BDM provides the smallest sizes, lowest temperatures, and highest phase space densities reported to date for magneto-optically trapped CaF molecules. We have also uncovered a mechanism that hinders further density enhancement via magnetic compression. We find low effective Λ-BDM trap depths that decrease with the strength of the magnetic gradient, leading to short lifetimes at high gradients. Looking ahead, BDMs could significantly aid the loading of molecules into optical tweezer arrays, which are a promising platform for quantum simulation and quantum information processing [1–4, 21, 22]. In addition, the enhanced densities could also aid the exploration of ultracold molecular collisions [18, 20] or provide better starting conditions for evaporative cooling. We conclude by contextualizing our BDM with those recently reported for YO [30] and SrF [20]. Despite different spin-rotation and hyperfine structure, we find that a CaF BDM is also possible. Specifically, the Λ-BDM robustly achieves sub-Doppler temperatures and substantially higher densities compared to a red MOT. This suggests that BDMs could be a powerful technique widely applicable to many laser-coolable molecules, including polyatomic ones such as CaOH and SrOH [10, 36–38]. ## I. METHODS

## A. Preparation of Molecules

CaF molecules are produced in a single-stage cryogenic buffer gas cell [1]. Molecules in the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) manifold are slowed via chirped slowing and loaded into a red-detuned DC magneto-optical trap (MOT) operating on the X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1) →A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) transition (λ = 606.3 nm) [2]. The MOT light contains four frequencies addressing the four ground hyperfine levels in X2Σ(v = 0, N = 1): |J, F⟩= |3/2, 2⟩, |3/2, 1⟩, |1/2, 0⟩and |1/2, 1⟩. As a shorthand, we will refer to the hyperfine levels by F and disambiguate |3/2, 1⟩and |1/2, 1⟩by labeling them F = 1+ and F = 1−, respectively. The excited hyperfine structure of the A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2, +) is unresolved. The four frequency components have single-photon frequency detunings of ∆+ (−2.3 MHz, 0, 0, −9.6 MHz), with ∆= 0.7 MHz. The single-photon frequency detunings are given with respect to the transitions to the excited hyperfine state of A2Π1/2(v = 0, J = 1/2), F = 1, mF = 0 . The relative power ratios are 5:3:1:3. The handedness of the F = 2 component is opposite to the three other ones. The MOT light is sent along three orthogonal directions (x, y, z). The beams in the horizontal plane (xyplane) are retro-reflected, while the two beams along the vertical direction (z) are sent in separately (Fig. S1). Each horizontal MOT beam has a total power of ∼22 mW with a beam waist (1/e2 radius) of ∼6 mm. The intensity of each vertical beam is matched to that of the radial beams to within 20%, and each vertical beam has a beam waist of ∼2.5 mm. The magnetic field gradient is generated using a pair of anti-Helmholtz coils, whose symmetry axis is along the z direction. This implies that the axial magnetic gradient B′ z = dBz/dz is related to the radial magnetic gradient B′ r = dBr/dr via B′ z = 2B′ r. The initial loading of molecules into the DC red-detuned MOT occurs for 5 ms at an axial magnetic gradient of B′ z = 26 G/cm. Subsequently, to compress the MOT, the gradient is linearly increased to B′ z = 104 G/cm and the MOT optical power

Initially, we observe significant shearing and movement of the BDM as the magnetic gradient is increased during the BDM compression stage. This limits the lifetime of the BDM and lengthens the equilibration timescale. We believe that this is due to power imbalances between opposing MOT beams, which leads to a slight offset of the BDM center position from the location of zero magnetic field. To counteract this effect, we ramp an external bias magnetic field in rough proportion to B′ z to ensure that the equilibrium BDM position remains largely fixed.

## B. Measuring Temperature

The temperature of the molecular cloud is determined via a time-of-flight measurement. The cloud is released from the MOT and expands freely for a variable time tm in the absence of light. It is then imaged using either Λ- cooling light or resonant light. For the data in Fig. 2(a) and Fig. 3(c), we image the cloud by applying Λ-cooling light for 30 ms. For Fig. 2(c) and (e), we resonantly image the cloud for 1 ms. A Gaussian fit is then applied to extract the sizes σz and σr as a function of tm, along the two directions ˆz and ˆr. The size versus time data is then fit with σ(t)2 = σ(0)2 + t2 m(kBT/m) to allow thermometry of the axial and radial directions.

C. Measuring F(B) for the Λ-BDM

To measure the Λ-BDM force versus magnetic field profile F(B) = ma(B), we first create a spatially small sample by loading molecules into a Λ-BDM at a magnetic gradient of B′ z = 22.9 G/cm. We then turn off the magnetic gradient and apply Λ-cooling in free space to obtain a low velocity spread. Subsequently, we apply a uniform magnetic field ⃗B = Bˆx and then optionally initialize the cloud with a finite velocity along ˆx using a beam resonant with the X −B transition (“push” beam in Fig. S1). We then switch on Λ-BDM light for a vari-

able duration t. The resulting velocity of the cloud after t is measured via time-of-flight with the following procedure. The cloud is allowed to evolve ballistically in the absence of light for a variable time tm, after which it is imaged with resonant light for 1 ms. We perform a Gaussian fit to extract the center-of-mass position xcm versus time tm. From a linear fit of xcm versus tm, the velocity for each Λ-BDM on-time t is obtained. For each B, we assume that the equation of motion obeyed by the molecules is m¨x = −mα(B) ˙x + F(B), consisting of a velocity damping term and a constant force. Note that we assume that both F and α are functions of B only (α is assumed to be constant over the velocity range explored). The equation-of-motion can be integrated to yield

v(t) = v∞+ (v(0) −v∞)e−αt, (1)

where v = ˙x and v∞= (F/m)/α is the terminal velocity. By measuring v as a function of the Λ-BDM on-time t at different magnetic fields B, both a(B) = F(B)/m and α(B) can be measured. To obtain good estimates of a(B) and α(B), we perform two sets of measurements with the molecules at two different initial velocities. First, after free space Λ-cooling, the cloud is already at rest (v(0) = 0). Alternatively, by applying a push beam resonant with the X −B transition for 4 µs, we can initialize the cloud at v(0) ≈200 mm/s. Because of the larger range of velocities explored, we find that precise estimates of α can be obtained from datasets with the push beam applied initially. On the other hand, precise estimates of v∞are obtained from datasets where the molecules start from rest. We therefore use the push beam datasets to first obtain α. Next, the terminal velocity v∞of an initially stationary cloud (no push applied) is obtained using data where the Λ- BDM light is applied for much longer than 1/α. This provides a good estimate of v∞. Finally, the extracted value of v∞is used to refit the push beam datasets to obtain a final estimate of the damping coefficient α.

## A. BDM Equilibration Time

We find rapid equilibration times on the 5 to 10 ms timescales for the four-frequency and two-frequency BDMs. At a gradient of B′ z = 14.6 G/cm, the fourfrequency BDM reaches its equilibrium size over a 1/e time of ∼10 ms (Fig. S2(a)). For measurements of the equilibrium size and temperature of the four-frequency BDM, the molecules are held for 35 ms at a gradient of B′ z = 14.6 G/cm to ensure that equilibrium is reached.

For the two-frequency Λ-BDM (B′ z = 33.3 G/cm, I optimized for maximum lifetime), an equilibrium size of ∼150 µm is reached over ∼5 ms (Fig. S2(b)). We believe the quicker equilibration time in the high-gradient two-frequency configuration is due to a higher restoring force resulting from a higher value of B′ z and I. We leave further exploration of equilibration times to future work. We note that for the images shown in main text Fig. 1(b), the Λ-BDM is directly loaded from the freespace Λ-cooled cloud (without stages 1-3) and is therefore far from equilibrium initially. Notably, even at 12 ms after initial loading (main text Fig. 1(b) lower right panel), which is longer than the measured 1/e equilibration time for small perturbations (Fig. S2(b)), the cloud has still not fully reached its final equilibrium size. In particular, even though the axial width is close to its equilibrium value, the radial width is still a factor ∼2 larger than the axial width; at equilibrium, the two widths are similar.

The number of molecules is measured by a 20 ms-long Λ-imaging pulse. After summing camera counts within an ROI, we convert the camera counts into the number of collected photons using known camera conversion factors. ## D. Effective Trap Potential

To quantitatively analyze Λ-BDM trapping, we assume that the force F(x) is derived from an effective conservative trapping potential U(x) that is Gaussian. We further assume that F is only a function of the local magnetic field B; hence the spatial dependence in the BDM arises from the magnetic gradient. In other words, F(x) = F(B(x)) = −∂U(B(x))/∂x = −U ′(B)B′, where B′ is the gradient. Assuming that U(x) is Gaussian in x and hence in B, the force can then be written as

F(B) = −ABe−B2/(2B2 0), (8)

where B0 is the magnetic field over which the force is significant and A is the overall amplitude. Using B = B′x and integrating with respect to x gives

U(x) = −AB2 0 B′ e−(B′x)2/(2B2 0) = −U0e−x2/(2d2) (9)

which shows that the maximum trap depth is given by U0 = AB2 0/B′, with a trap size given by d = B0/B′.

## V. ESTIMATING BDM LIFETIME VERSUS MAGNETIC FIELD GRADIENT

In this section, we provide details on how we use the experimentally measured acceleration curve a(B), damping curve α(B), and the measured dependences of T and σ on gradient B′ z to estimate the lifetime of the Λ-BDM. In the main text, the resulting estimate is shown in the inset of Fig. 4(e). As explained in the main text, we describe a(B) via the force F = m a(B) derived from an effective conservative Gaussian potential U(x) = −U0 exp � −x2/(2d2)  , where m is the molecular mass and U0 is the peak effective trap depth. We assume that the spatial dependence arises from the magnetic gradient, which is expected to be accurate at low gradients where the effective motional magnetic fields are negligible compared to the mean magnetic field experienced by the molecules. We assume that the acceleration curves are identical for the radial and axial directions. This is partially justified by the similar values of

the measured spring constants per gradient near B′ z = 0 shown in Fig. 3(d) of the main text (See Section VII). To estimate lifetimes, we first find a smooth interpolation of the measured values of the widths (σr, σz) and temperatures (Tr, Tz) versus the axial magnetic gradient B′ z. We find that a linear model for Tr and Tz describes the data well (Fig. 3(b) in main text). For the widths, we fit the observed widths to a phenomenological model of σ(B′ z) = a + b/xc. Next, we perform a Monte-Carlo simulation for a grid of axial gradient values up to 40 G. For each gradient, we create 104 instances of axial positions r and radial positions z. These radial (axial) positions satisfy a normal distribution with variance given by σr (σz) obtained from the smoothed model above. We treat the radial and axial positions independently. For each radial position, we compute the local magnetic field by multiplying by the radial magnetic gradient B′ r = B′ z/2. Similarly, for each axial position, we compute the local magnetic field by multiplying by the axial magnetic gradient B′ z. Having found the local magnetic field, we obtain the local damping rate α from α(B). We also determine the local trap depth U0, which is obtained from the measured a(B) curve. Note that U0 depends on the local magnetic field and also the gradient. Once Ueff,r(Ueff,z) is computed for each radial (axial) position, we compute a list of ηr = kBTr/Ueff,r (ηz = kBTz/Ueff,z) for each instance. For each value of axial gradient, Tr an Tz are obtained from the linear fits to measured data. For each axial gradient value, which has 104 radial and 104 axial points, we can then perform ensemble averages for the mean damping rates ⟨α⟩and mean temperature-to-trap depth ratio ⟨η⟩. In Fig. S6(a)and Fig. 4(d) in the main text, we show the mean damping rates ⟨αr⟩and ⟨αz⟩along the radial and axial directions, respectively. In Fig. S6(b) and Fig 4(e) in the main text, we show the mean temperature-to-trapdepth ratio ⟨ηr⟩and ⟨ηz⟩along the radial and axial directions, respectively. Here angle brackets indicate an ensemble average over the different spatial positions within the trap. One can see that over axial gradients ranging from 5 G/cm to 40 G/cm, ⟨αr⟩and ⟨αz⟩do not vary by more than 20%. On the other hand, ⟨ηr⟩and ⟨ηz⟩vary much more. ⟨ηz⟩can even exceed unity above 30 G/cm. Finally, to semi-quantitatively estimate the loss rate, we use the following picture. We assume that particles thermalize with the cooling light locally and that particles above the local trap depth are lost. For a thermal ensemble, the fraction of particles above the local trap depth is given by exp(−1/η). At the same time, the thermalization rate is given by the damping rate α. Therefore, we can estimate the total escape rate as γ = C ⟨2γesc,r + γesc,z⟩, where γesc,r = ⟨αr exp(−1/ηr)⟩ is the radial escape rate, γesc,z = ⟨αz exp(−1/ηz)⟩is the axial escape rate, and C is a constant of order O(0.1). C is used to phenomenologically capture the time needed to repopulate the tails of a thermal distribution, and to encode a slowing-down factor because hot particles have

a finite probability of being recaptured before leaving the MOT. In Fig. S6(c), we show the mean escape rates ⟨γesc,z⟩and ⟨γesc,r⟩along the axial and radial directions, respectively. One observes that the axial escape rate is much higher and is the dominant escape channel. This is primarily because the axial gradient is twice as high as the radial gradient in a quadrupole magnetic field, leading to a lower axial trap depth. In addition, as shown in Fig. 3(b) in the main text, the axial temperature is also observed to be higher, partially contributing to the higher axial escape rate. In addition to the above loss mechanism, there is also a background loss due to off-resonant scattering into other vibrational and rotational states that are not repumped and also finite vacuum lifetime. This can be taken into account with a background loss rate γbkg. The total loss rate can then be estimated as

γtot = γ + γbkg. (10)

At high loss rates, the measured lifetime is limited by the time it takes for a particle to escape the MOT region. To take this into account, we phenomenologically add to the estimated lifetime a constant diffusion time τdiff. The observed lifetime can then be estimated as

τ = 1 γ + γbkg + τdiff (11)

In Fig. S6(d), we show the observed lifetime τ as a function of the axial gradient B′ z, along with a fit with the model above (shown in red). We find qualitative agreement. Regarding γbkg, if we attribute this entirely to decay into un-repumped states during optical cycling, the corresponding number of photons scattered is 1.1(3)×105. Regarding τdiff, the fitted value is not consistent with diffusive motion at T ≈100 µK. In detail, if one assumes diffusive motion, the time t required to exit the BDM can be estimated as t ∼d2Γsc/¯v2, where d is the size of the trap and ¯v is the typical velocity. With d = 0.5 mm and T = 100 µK, this timescale is ∼5 s. Possible explanations of the much shorter timescale could be because of an imbalance in beam intensities between opposing pairs of BDM beams that lead to a net force at large magnetic fields. With regards to C, as discussed previously, we expect C to be on the order of 0.1. The fitted value is consistent with this expectation. ## B. Validating the Einstein Relation Between Damping Rate and Scattering Rate

As derived in Section IVA and used in previous work with BDMs of YO [10], one can use an Einstein relation to relate the momentum diffusion rate to the damping coefficient α. Since the momentum diffusion rate is determined by the scattering rate Γsc, this produces an Einstein relation between Γsc and α, which reads

ℏ2k2 LΓsc 3mα = kBT, (14)

where kL is the wavenumber of the cooling light. We can verify that the Einstein relation is satisfied by computing the ratio ζ = ℏ2k2Γsc 3mαkBT from measured quantities. The relation is satisfied when ζ = 1. # Bichromatic Imaging of Single Molecules in an Optical Tweezer Array

Connor M. Holland,1 Yukai Lu,1, 2 and Lawrence W. Cheuk1, ∗

1Department of Physics, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA 2Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544 USA (Dated: August 26, 2022)

We report on a novel bichromatic ﬂuorescent imaging scheme for background-free detection of single CaF molecules trapped in an optical tweezer array. By collecting ﬂuorescence on one optical transition while using another for laser-cooling, we achieve an imaging ﬁdelity of 97.7(2)% and a non-destructive detection ﬁdelity of 95.5(6)%. We characterize loss mechanisms of our scheme, many of which are generically relevant to the ﬂuorescent detection of trapped molecules, including two-photon decay and admixtures of higher excited states that are induced by the trapping light.

Single molecules trapped in rearrangeable arrays of optical tweezers have been proposed as a platform for quantum simulation, quantum information processing, and precision measurements [1–4]. Compared to the platform of neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays [5–9], which has been very successful in a wide variety of quantum applications [10–16], molecules in tweezer arrays offer new capabilities thanks to their rich internal structure and long-range electric dipolar interactions in long-lived states [17, 18]. These features have spurred experimental eﬀorts to create single molecules in tweezer arrays via coherent assembly from constituent atoms [19–23] and through direct laser-cooling [24–26]. The latter approach of directly laser-cooling has the advantage of potentially higher loading rates and higher detection ﬁdelities, because individual molecules can be directly cooled and read out optically through cycling hundreds of photons. Crucially, it appears to be a general technique that could be extended to polyatomic molecules [27–31]. Laser-cooled molecules in optical tweezers may be non-destructively detected through ﬂuorescent imaging. However, because optical tweezers have limited trap depths, cooling is needed to counteract the recoil heating due to photon scattering. To date, Λ-imaging has been the only technique that provides both cooling and the ﬂuorescence needed to detect single molecules [24, 32]. Nevertheless, it comes with a side eﬀect. Stray laser-cooling light can lead to signiﬁcant detection backgrounds that reduce detection ﬁdelities. A strategy to circumvent this problem is to use two optical transitions, one for lasercooling and the other for inducing ﬂuorescence. In such a bichromatic scheme, background-free detection can be achieved by spectrally ﬁltering out stray laser-cooling light. This approach has been successfully used to image single atoms in optical lattices and optical tweezers [7–9, 33–35]. For molecules, bichromatic imaging schemes have also been demonstrated for laser-cooled ensembles [31, 36], but not with single molecule resolution. In this paper, we demonstrate a high-ﬁdelity bichromatic imaging scheme for single CaF molecules trapped in optical tweezers. Our work starts with laser-cooled CaF loaded from a magneto-optical trap [37, 38] into a

The resulting X −B ﬂuorescence is collected through the microscope objective and imaged onto an EMCCD camera with an overall eﬃciency of 0.049(2). Dichroic ﬁlters in the imaging path remove the Λ-cooling light, X −A ﬂuorescence, and stray optical tweezer light. As shown in Fig. 1(c), the average images obtained using bichromatic imaging reveal the presence of molecules in the optical tweezer array. Optimizing for maximal survival at a ﬁxed X −B light intensity of I = 12(1)mW/cm2, we ﬁnd Λ- cooling parameters similar to those previously reported for Λ-imaging [24]. At optimal parameters, we obtain an imaging lifetime of τ = 148(14) ms, and a X −B photon scattering rate of Γsc = 1.95(4) × 104 s−1. To evaluate the imaging performance, we ﬁrst construct histograms of the total camera counts in cropped image regions surrounding each tweezer (Fig. 1(c)). The histograms reveal a bimodal distribution (Fig. 1(d)), with the two peaks corresponding to tweezer instances that are empty and occupied. We classify tweezer instances below (above) a threshold θ as empty (occupied). We describe the classiﬁcation errors by two probabilities, ϵ10 and ϵ01, which correspond to the probabilities of incorrectly classifying an occupied tweezer as empty and vice versa. The total misclassiﬁcation probability is dependent on the average occupation p and is given by ϵ(p) = p ϵ10+(1−p)ϵ01. We deﬁne the imaging ﬁdelity f as probability of correctly classifying a tweezer when the occupation probability is 0.5, i.e. f = 1 −ϵopt(0.5), at the optimal threshold θopt. By applying a rescaling procedure to histograms (details in [40]), we obtain the classiﬁcation errors ϵ10 and ϵ01 for 30 ms-long images, from which we extract an imaging ﬁdelity of f = 0.977(2) (Fig. 2(a)). During the images, ≈35 photons are collected per molecule, which is well above the background of ≈0.3 photons per tweezer. A second metric for single molecule detection is the non-destructive detection ﬁdelity fND, which we deﬁne as the probability that a tweezer initially classiﬁed as occupied remains occupied following imaging. This metric is relevant to rearranging molecules into defect-free arrays, since the success probability of creating an array of size N is limited by (fND)N. Unlike the imaging ﬁdelity f, the non-destructive detection ﬁdelity fND primarily depends on ϵ01, which is approximately equivalent to the false-positive rate. The detection threshold θ can therefore be increased to reduce ϵ01 at the expense of increasing ϵ10, which is the probability of rejecting occupied tweezers. In addition to the classiﬁcation errors ϵ10 and ϵ01, fND is also aﬀected by the survival probability of molecules following detection. Thus, the imaging duration should be chosen to balance between minimizing imaging loss and maximizing molecular ﬂuorescence;
